So, what we do, basically, is we sit in the middle. Your core banking system stays exactly where it is. We do not touch it. On one side you have your core, and on the other side you have the networks, the correspondent banks, the new instant rails, and today every one of those connections is built by hand, one by one, and every one of them breaks in its own way. Our middleware is one layer between the two. You connect once, to us, and we translate the messages into whatever format the other side needs. The typical bank we work with has something like forty point-to-point connections, and after eighteen months it has one. And the part people usually miss, honestly, is reconciliation. Because everything passes through one layer, the matching happens in real time, so your operations team stops spending the morning finding out what happened yesterday.

If you ask me what slows down cross-border payments in Europe, I would not say technology. The technology is mostly there. What slows us down is that every jurisdiction wants to see the same payment in a slightly different way. The same transfer from Frankfurt to Sao Paulo is checked against sanctions lists in Germany, then reported in one format to one regulator and in another format to another, and if one field is missing, the whole thing stops and a person has to look at it. We did a count last year. Around one payment in eight needed a human being somewhere along the way, and almost always for a data problem, not for a real risk. So when people talk about instant payments, I always ask the same question. Instant for whom? The money can move in seconds. The paperwork around it still moves at the speed of the slowest regulator.

Three numbers, and then I will let you get to your coffee. Number one. Ten years ago, a business payment from one continent to another took between two and five days. Today, the majority arrive within an hour, and a large share arrive in minutes. Number two. The cost has not come down anywhere near as fast. For a small business sending a few thousand dollars, the total cost, the fees plus the exchange rate margin, is still several percent, and that is the number that decides whether a small exporter in Brazil or Vietnam can compete at all. Number three, and this is the one I want you to take home. The fastest-growing part of this market is not the big corporates. It is the small and mid-sized companies that were never profitable to serve before. Whoever makes that segment cheap to serve is going to write the next chapter of this industry. That's it. Enjoy the coffee.
